findings.evidence: The proof itself derives `have hT0 : (0 : ℝ) ∈ T := hT.mem hTne` (line 334), and `0 ∈ pathParameters S x v ↔ x ∈ S` by `mem_pathParameters` (line 104).
findings.fix: Reword to "i.e. the production point lies in `S` and the ray does not re-enter `S` once it has left it".
findings.issue: The gloss "When the path parameters are star-shaped about `0`, i.e. the ray does not re-enter `S` once it has left it" is not equivalent to the hypothesis: `StarConvex ℝ 0 (pathParameters S x v)` also forces `x ∈ S`. A reader taking the "i.e." at face value would expect the lemma to apply with `x ∉ S` (e.g. path parameters `Icc 1 2`, where the length is 1 but `sSup` is 2).

findings.evidence: `densityWeightedPathLength ρ ρ₀ x v = ρ₀⁻¹ * ∫ s in Ici 0, ρ (x + s • v)` (line 130-131) integrates in `s`, not arc length; `geometricPathLength`'s docstring at line 116 carries the qualifier the others lack.
findings.fix: Add the `‖v‖ = 1` qualifier to each of these three physical readings, as the `geometricPathLength` definition docstring already does.
findings.issue: "the length of a uniform medium of density `ρ₀` containing as many nucleons per unit transverse area along the ray as `ρ` does" holds only for `‖v‖ = 1`; the integral is over the parameter `s`, so it is off by `‖v‖` otherwise. Same uncaveated reading at line 19-20 ("the length of the part of the ray that lies in the set `S`") and line 26-27 ("the same number of nucleons per unit area along the ray"). The `geometricPathLength` docstring (line 116) correctly says "and `‖v‖ = 1`".

findings.evidence: `theorem pathParameters_closedBall {c x v : F} {R : ℝ} (hx : x ∈ closedBall c R)` (line 370); `open MeasureTheory Metric Set` (line 88).
findings.fix: Write "a point `x` of the ball", matching the theorem docstrings at lines 367 and 397 ("a point `x` of the closed ball of radius `R` about `c`").
findings.issue: Main results says "the path parameters from a point `x` of the sphere", but the hypothesis is `hx : x ∈ closedBall c R`. With `open Metric` in this file, `sphere` names the boundary `Metric.sphere`, so this reads as a strictly stronger hypothesis than the theorem requires.

summary: The module docstring and most declaration docstrings are accurate and mathematically motivated, with no roadmap or process narrative. Three docstrings state the mathematics inaccurately: the star-convexity gloss on `geometricPathLength_eq_sSup`, the uncaveated physical reading of the integral for a non-unit direction, and "sphere" where the hypothesis is the closed ball.
